parse._why: Uber labels every leg of a journey — away, trip, total — and prints its distance beside its time. A minutes-only token with no label is not a leg at all, and the card is full of them. parse.name: ...whatever invisible character stands in for its space
parse._why: Python's \s is Unicode and JavaScript's is not, and they disagree about exactly six characters. normalize() collapses \s+ in both ports, so a card carrying one of them arrives as two different strings and every rule downstream reads a different card. U+0085 made the browser publish this road as a $22 offer while the Pi refused it; U+FEFF did it the other way round. No card on file carries any of the six: a hole closed rather than a bug repaired, and these six keep it closed.

parse._why: The single-leg half of legs_short_a_distance, which the old count exemption hid. The reading keeps the journey's whole time against no distance at all, which flatters the rate, so it is doubted rather than published: milesUncertain makes rate() charge no mileage and cap the verdict at CLOSE CALL. What tells this from a real total is the bracket — a total prints none where a distance would go.
parse.text: $16.05 25 min (11.q5 mi) total

parse.name: ...on a labelled lone leg too, since the label decides nothing
parse._why: The clause asks lostMiles, not labelled. A card that labelled its only leg still says nothing about whether a distance was ever printed beside it — and a total is exactly that shape, labelled and distanceless.
parse.text: $16.05 25 min (11.q5 mi) trip

parse.name: ...and the corpus card the single-leg clause was measured on
parse._why: Verbatim damage out of the journal rather than an invention: the distance read as (g3 mi), so the leg kept its 26 minutes and lost its miles entirely. 335 of the 337 damaged readings that still published an optimistic rate after the two-leg hole was closed had this shape.
parse.text: $7.06 Guaranteed (incl. tip) 26 min (g3 mi) total Taco Mac

parse.name: ...but a lone leg whose distance was recovered elsewhere is certain
parse._why: The `miles is None` guard, and the reason the clause is not simply 'one leg with lostMiles'. The bracket here holds a plus, which defeats the leg's own distance group, and the lone-distance branch in parse() then recovers 7.2 correctly. This is why the question is asked BELOW that branch rather than beside the leg sum, where the answer would still have been no. Doubting this would throw away a good number, which this project treats as exactly as bad as publishing a wrong one.

rate.name: ...and with no running cost configured there is nothing to cap
rate._why: costPerMile 0 means the driver has opted out of costing, so gross IS net and the rate is the offer rather than a ceiling on it.

rate.name: ...and the verdict is judged on the distance the repair produced
rate._why: The same card with less time left. 24 mi over the 19 minutes to the deadline is 75.8 mph, which doubt() refuses — but the reading published is the REPAIRED 2.4 mi, and that is what the verdict must be reached with. This pinned nothing until it was written down: rate() passed the recovered distance in Python and the original one in JavaScript, so the Pi showed CLOSE CALL and the browser showed no verdict at all for the same card on the same clock. The fixture above misses it because 25 minutes puts the original under doubt()'s speed limit, and because it never asserts `state`.

rate.name: a delivery distance that lost its decimal is recovered against the deadline
rate._why: A delivery card states a distance with no time beside it, so parse() had no denominator and check_distance returned it untouched. 2.4 mi read as 24 mi was charged $7.20 of mileage instead of $0.72 — $18.1/hr shown as $2.5/hr, unflagged. rate() knows the clock.
rate.text: $8.25 Guaranteed (incl. tip) 24 mi Deliver by 6:05 PM

rate.name: ...and the same card read correctly is left alone
rate.text: $8.25 Guaranteed (incl. tip) 2.4 mi Deliver by 6:05 PM

rate.name: ...and a printed decimal is not 'recovered' away
rate._why: The decimal point is what says whether one was lost, and it has to be tested where it decides the answer: 60.0 miles with 25 minutes to run is 144 mph, so the recovery WOULD fire and turn it into 6.0 — the printed decimal is the only thing stopping it. The card is doubted instead, which is the honest answer to a distance that cannot be right and cannot be explained by a lost point. A 10.0 mi card at an ordinary speed proves nothing here, because check_distance never reaches the recovery at all.
rate.text: $8.25 Guaranteed (incl. tip) 60.0 mi Deliver by 6:05 PM

rate.name: a delivery distance plausible against its deadline is not touched
rate._why: 24 miles with 45 minutes to run is 32 mph and perfectly ordinary. The recovery only fires on a speed that cannot be true.
rate.text: $18.00 Guaranteed (incl. tip) 24 mi Deliver by 6:25 PM

rate.name: a ride card is checked by parse() and not re-checked here

rate.name: a card that lost a leg is not a $310/hr ACCEPT
rate._why: This card is already in the parse fixtures: the '53L min' leg is correctly dropped as rubbish, which leaves the 9-minute pickup leg carrying the whole payout. It parses complete, is_whole is False, and it rated as a green ACCEPT at $310.67/hr where the truth over 62 minutes is $46. A lost leg makes pay, minutes and miles each individually plausible — it is the rate they imply together that cannot be true, which is what the continuous ceiling now sees.

_coerce_comment: The three functions that decide what an offer is judged against, checked in both languages from one list. Every one of these had drifted: Number('  ') is 0 in JavaScript so a whitespace target meant every offer was an ACCEPT while Python fell back to 25; float() takes '1e3' and '1_0' and parseFloat does not; and Infinity and NaN were guarded out of doubt() in JavaScript and compared against the bounds in Python. None of it was reachable from a test. '@inf', '@-inf' and '@nan' stand in for values JSON cannot hold.

doubt._why: $1.36 read as $136 is $816/hr over ten minutes. Each half is sane on its own — $136 is inside SANE_PAY, ten minutes inside SANE_MINUTES — and nothing tested the pair, so five readings of one real shift reached the panel as ACCEPT at between $103 and $816 an hour.

doubt.name: ...and the same card read correctly is not doubted
a short hop that really does pay well is not a misread
doubt._why: $/hr is unbounded as the duration shrinks, so a bare rate ceiling clips real offers. $10 over two minutes is $300/hr and ordinary; the ceiling applies only once the trip is long enough for a rate to describe it.

doubt.name: ...and just past the boundary the same rate is impossible
doubt._why: $50 over ten minutes is $300/hr for a trip long enough that the rate means something. No app pays it.

doubt.name: an hour's work at a plausible rate is not doubted
the ceiling does not loosen as the trip gets shorter
doubt._why: Written as two branches, the guard was a STEP: below ten minutes nothing but SANE_PAY's own $300 applied, so $136 over ten minutes was doubted while the same $136 over NINE was a green ACCEPT at $899/hr. A guard a shorter trip walks under is not a guard.

doubt.name: ...and the boundary payout itself is still allowed
doubt._why: $33.33 is the payout that reaches SANE_RATE at ten minutes, so it is the flat cap below the boundary. The bound has to admit its own boundary value or it is a tighter bound than it says it is.

doubt.name: ...while a dollar past it is not
a five dollar errand over three minutes is an ordinary offer
doubt._why: The largest sub-ten-minute payout across 568 real offers is $5.00. A cap that refused this would be the guard-clips-a-real-offer failure, which costs exactly as much as letting a misread through.

_deadline_comment: A delivery deadline is minutes since midnight, and the duration it implies depends on the time of day — so parse() reports the clock time and rate() does the subtraction. Checked separately because a parser that reads the clock cannot be held to a fixed corpus.

deadline.name: no half of the day stated

_until_comment: Minutes left, wrapping midnight. A deadline already past is a stale card, not a short job, and the sanity bounds refuse what wrapping turns it into.
_address_comment: A full street address off the screen that comes AFTER the accept. An offer card never carries one - Uber prints "Customer dropoff" and no address on 106 of this driver's 604 cards, 18% of everything the rig sees, and that drives 39% of the pairs where the stacking advice can say nothing. `expect` is [line, city, zip], or null when the reading is refused. It refuses far more readily than anything else in this file and on purpose: every other rule reads a card the driver can also see and decides a number they can sanity-check, while this fills in a fact they cannot check later, against an offer that has not arrived yet.

address.name: a plain address, as a screen would print it
...on two lines, which is how a screen really prints it
address._why: normalize() joins the lines with a space, so there is no comma between the street and the town and no grammar for where one stops. The USPS suffix is what splits it. Without that the town comes out as "Daffodil Ln Powder Springs" and two readings of the same street disagree about where they are.
address.text: Deliver to 1234 Daffodil Ln Powder Springs, GA 30127 Navigate

address.name: ...with a quadrant, which belongs to the street and not the town
a town that contains a street suffix splits at the later one
address._why: "900 Powder Springs Rd Marietta" has two candidate breaks and only the second is real.

address.name: a street with two suffixes splits at the last one
address._why: "Mill Run Ct" is an ordinary street name and it contains two of the USPS suffixes. Splitting at the first leaves the town as "Ct Marietta", which compares unequal to every other reading of Marietta. Only the LAST one is the real break - the same reasoning as the town that contains a suffix, from the other direction.

address.name: a ZIP+4 keeps the five that matter
a ZIP spelled in stand-ins is still that ZIP
address._why: Five characters of small type through a lens: "3O127" is this OCR's commonest confusion, not a different number. The STATE gets no such help - see the case below.

address.name: a state that did not read is refused, not corrected
address._why: The state is the check, so repairing it would be inventing the one token that is here to refuse. "6A" is not Georgia; it is a reading that failed, and the driver can press the button again.

address.name: two letters that are not a state are not a state
five digits that are not a ZIP are not a ZIP
the last address on the screen is the one you are going to
address._why: A navigation screen shows where you are going, and a pickup already made comes above it. The street must not reach back across the earlier ZIP either: "...GA 30339 then 12 Oak Ln" was stored as the street.
address.text: pickup 900 Battery Ave SE, Atlanta, GA 30339 then 12 Oak Ln, Marietta, GA 30060

address.name: a stray letter in front of the town is the icon row, not a word
address._why: "l Atlanta", "j Powder Springs" - PLACE_TOWN in advice.js tolerates exactly this, and the two have to agree about what a town is called or the same place read twice compares unequal to itself.
address.text: 800 Forrest St NW, l Atlanta, GA 30318

address.name: ...and the icon row is stripped on the no-comma path too
address._why: The stray letter is stripped when the address printed its own comma, and was not when the street suffix had to split it - which is the path this parser calls the case to EXPECT, since a screen puts the street and the town on two lines and normalize joins them with a space. The town then read as 'l Atlanta', which PLACE_TOWN in advice.js cannot parse at all: its junk allowance covers a single uppercase letter, not a lowercase one. area() returned no town and the geography went silent on exactly the orders the scan was added to rescue.
address.text: 800 Forrest St NW l Atlanta, GA 30318

The moment one loses its distance it drops out of the set legs_short_a_distance counts, the count falls to one, and the rule written for exactly this damage returned False. Measured: it fired on ONE of 604 real cards and on none of 1080 readings with a leg's distance broken. whole._why: Nothing is asked about what is inside the bracket, and requiring a digit there sounds like a second belt but is a hole: the number is exactly what the damage removes. Measured over 3466 readings damaged four ways, the digit clause halved what this rule caught - 2096 down to 1052 - and bought nothing, since both versions fire on zero of the 604 clean cards.

whole.name: damage that lands on the digits is caught too
whole._why: The tail test can only ever see a bracket the LEG regex FAILED to consume, so it catches damage on the unit - (8.1 m1) - and was blind to damage on the DIGITS, which is the class this rule was written for. Here a 1 is read as an L, which this parser calls the commonest single confusion there is: DC accepts the L, the bracket is swallowed by the match, the tail begins at the address, and the leg dropped silently out of the journey. 17 minutes were charged against 1.8 of the journey's 9.9 miles, whole and unflagged, a green $72.49/hr where the truth is $63.92.

What tells a damaged leg from a wait line is a bracket holding a digit sitting where the distance would be, and it has to be the FIRST thing after the minutes - because a bracket appears in this wait line's tail too, belonging to the leg after it. Searching the tail loosely instead fires on 43% of clean cards.

Doubting it would throw away a good number, which is the same failure pointed the other way. This is the whole risk the clause carries.
